name: Malicious Cable Detector by O.MG
one_line: Inline dongle: plug a suspect USB cable into it, then it into a host port. Samples the cable's power draw 200,000 times/sec and uses side-channel power analysis to flag known malicious cables (including O.MG Cables, which show no signal on the data lines until triggered); also blocks the data lines so the port-side device can charge safely.
why_notable: Purpose-built defensive counter-tool for BadUSB/O.MG-style cable implants; no equivalent detector is currently in the tracked list.

name: O.MG Programmer USB A+C
one_line: USB dongle used to do initial setup/provisioning, flash firmware updates, recover a unit after self-destruct, and pull forensic dumps/backups from any O.MG Cable, Plug, Adapter, or UnBlocker; one programmer works across the whole O.MG device family.
why_notable: Distinct standalone accessory (own SKU/page) that is the required tool for reflashing and forensically imaging the O.MG implant line — not a cable, case, or sticker.

name: O.MG Cable, Woven (Elite, USB-C/USB-C, Black or White)
one_line: Same Elite O.MG Cable electronics (Wi-Fi-controlled keystroke-injection/exfil implant hidden in a USB cable) as the base O.MG Cable, but the outer jacket is braided/woven fabric instead of standard TPE plastic. USB-C to USB-C, directional connector only.
why_notable: New SKU/jacket variant of the O.MG Cable, flagged as 'New' on the site as of this check; flagging for a human to confirm it's cosmetic/durability-only and not a new hardware revision.

name: Glytch GPS Mod for Pager
one_line: 3D-printed, hand-assembled add-on board carrying a Quectel LC86 multi-constellation GNSS chipset that clips onto the WiFi Pineapple Pager to geotag its Wi-Fi survey/attack logs.
why_notable: Standalone-sellable hardware module (own chipset, own SKU) rather than a cable/case, adding a sensor capability the base Pager doesn't have.

name: Glytch Ethernet Mod for Pager
one_line: 3D-printed, hand-assembled add-on board using an RTL8152B USB-to-Ethernet chip that clips onto the WiFi Pineapple Pager to give it a wired RJ45 network port.
why_notable: Sold as a standalone accessory for the Pager line, but the chip itself is a stock USB-Ethernet controller with no security-specific circuitry — closer to the 'generic adapter' exclusion than the other two Glytch mods.

name: Glytch Mesh Mod for Pager
one_line: 3D-printed, hand-assembled add-on board with an 868/900 MHz radio and integrated antenna that clips onto the WiFi Pineapple Pager to add sub-GHz mesh-networking connectivity.
why_notable: Standalone sub-GHz radio module giving an already-tracked device off-grid mesh comms capability it doesn't otherwise have.

name: Opera Cake for HackRF
one_line: Add-on board for HackRF that routes two SMA ports to any of eight secondary antenna/filter ports (1x8 or dual 1x4 switching), 1 MHz-4 GHz, switchable by frequency or time via existing HackRF software (hackrf_sweep etc.).
why_notable: Only currently-sold GSG accessory that adds automated multi-antenna/filter-bank switching to HackRF, not a bundle repackaging an already-tracked board.

name: URTI (Universal Radio Test Instrument)
one_line: In-development wideband full-duplex SDR platform with integrated directional coupler, intended to work as spectrum analyzer, VNA, vector signal gen/analyzer, antenna analyzer, power meter, and frequency counter in one device.
why_notable: Open-source GSG project (ARDC/TAPR funded) with a live product page but no listed price and not yet released for purchase; worth a human check-in on release status.

name: ChipWhisperer-HuskyPlus
one_line: Side-channel capture/glitching board: 250 MS/s 12-bit ADC, Artix-7A100T FPGA with 327,828-sample buffer, programmable clock/voltage glitch injection, logic-analyzer triggering (pattern match, UART, ARM trace).
why_notable: Distinct higher-spec model above the already-tracked ChipWhisperer-Husky (larger FPGA/buffer, different price tier), sold as its own SKU.

name: ChipSHOVER
one_line: Motorized 3-axis (XYZ) positioning stage, 5 cm travel per axis, better than 200 nm precision / 4 um repeatability, for precisely placing EM fault-injection probes or side-channel sensors over a die; controlled from an LCD panel or Python.
why_notable: New product category for NewAE (precision robotic positioner for chip-level probing), not a variant of any already-tracked device.

name: CW308 UFO Board
one_line: Baseboard providing shared power supplies (1.2-3.5V), oscillator/crystal socket, on-board filtering for clean power measurement, and diode-protected I/O for voltage glitching, that accepts swappable target daughtercards (8-bit, 32-bit MCU, FPGA).
why_notable: The standard target platform for ChipWhisperer side-channel/glitching work; explicitly named as a gap to check in the assignment. Currently listed out of stock.

name: PhyWhisperer-USB (CW610)
one_line: In-line USB 2.0 (LS/FS/HS) monitor and trigger box with a Spartan FPGA and 240 MHz clock; sits between host and device, buffers 8,192 bytes of traffic, fires a trigger on matched data patterns, has a built-in power shunt and a front-panel power-cycle button, and can feed sync clock/trigger to ChipWhisperer capture hardware. Reported twice: $360.00 direct from newae.com, and $365 via Crowd Supply (https://www.crowdsupply.com/newae/phywhisperer-usb) — same product, two prices seen, not resolved to a single figure.
why_notable: Standalone USB protocol-triggered instrument used to time power-analysis/fault-injection captures against USB-connected targets; distinct from any tracked device; sold through two channels at slightly different prices.

name: CW310 "Bergen Board" (Large FPGA, K410T)
one_line: FPGA evaluation/target board built around a Xilinx Kintex K410T, with a supervisory MCU for config/temp/voltage/clock control, DDR3+SRAM, JTAG/USB/PMOD headers, multi-stage VCC-INT filtering plus inductive shunt and LNA for power analysis, and SMA/fan access for EM fault injection.
why_notable: Large-FPGA target board for full system-on-chip/crypto-core emulation in side-channel research; too big to be a bundle repackaging of an already-tracked item. Currently out of stock (supply chain).

name: CW312T-RP2350
one_line: Target board carrying a Raspberry Pi RP2350 (dual-core ARM+RISC-V) with an external voltage regulator bypassing the chip's internal one, for power-analysis and fault-injection/glitch-detector testing against that MCU.
why_notable: Standalone target board for a current, widely-used MCU (RP2350/Pico 2 family), a distinct SKU rather than a bundle.

name: SAM4S CW313 Target
one_line: Target board with a populated Microchip ATSAM4S2 (ARM Cortex-M4, 128KB flash/64KB SRAM, 1.2V core), programmable via serial bootloader or JTAG, for running crypto code under ChipWhisperer power/fault analysis (requires a CW313 baseboard).
why_notable: A populated (not empty-socket) MCU target board sold as its own SKU, distinct from the already-tracked capture units.

name: Probe Set with Power Supply
one_line: Isolated power module (5V USB in, +3.3V for LNA, +-7.8V for differential probe, up to 50V isolation) sold with a differential probe, an LNA probe, and an H-field probe for measuring/picking up power and EM signals off a chip during side-channel testing.
why_notable: Provides physical EM/power probes not covered by any already-tracked capture board; flagged borderline because it's closer to sensing accessories than a full standalone instrument.

name: Socket Target for CW308 (STM32F-SOCKET64)
one_line: CW308 daughtercard with an empty TQFP-64 ZIF socket and a switch selecting two pinout configurations, for socketing user-supplied STM32F (Cortex-M0/M3/M4) chips for side-channel/glitch testing without soldering; no MCU included.
why_notable: Flagged borderline: it's a bare socket/adapter card (no populated chip) for the already-tracked CW308 ecosystem, closer to the 'generic adapter' exclusion than a standalone tool — include for human judgment call.

name: Diabolic Drive
one_line: USB flash-drive-form-factor device that behaves as normal 64GB storage until wirelessly (Wi-Fi) commanded to expose a HID keyboard interface and inject a stored keystroke payload; spoofs VID/PID/serial for both the storage and HID personas.
why_notable: Off-the-shelf combination of flash storage, remote-triggered HID injection, and hardware-ID spoofing in one drive; not currently in the tracked list.

name: Diabolic Parasite
one_line: Inline USB implant: you unplug an existing keyboard/mouse, connect it to the Parasite's female USB port, and plug the Parasite into the freed port; it clones the passthrough device's hardware identity, logs keystrokes to a web UI, and can wirelessly trigger keystroke injection with randomized typing cadence and ALT+Numpad layout bypass.
why_notable: Combines passive keylogging, passthrough device-identity cloning, and remote keystroke injection in one covert in-line implant, aimed explicitly at red-team USB assessments.

name: ProxmarkPro
one_line: Standalone handheld RFID/NFC reader (LCD, nav switch, swappable antennas, microSD) that can identify, save/load, clone-to-T5577, emulate, and brute-force HID/EM4100/Mifare tags without a tethered computer; listed price options ranged $55-$400 depending on configuration, so no single price was recorded.
why_notable: A separate commercial 'Proxmark' handheld line from a different vendor (Rysc Corp) than the RRG/Iceman hardware behind the tracked Proxmark models; overlaps enough in name and function to need a human check against the existing Proxmark entries.

name: OpticSpy
one_line: Photodiode receiver module that converts visible/near-IR optical signals into a digital serial stream over USB, for finding and decoding optical covert channels, blinkenlight data exfiltration, and IR remote signals.
why_notable: Purpose-built tool for TEMPEST-style optical covert-channel discovery and data exfiltration research, a niche not covered by anything currently tracked.

name: UsbSafe²
one_line: Inline USB dongle with a physical button that can disable the USB data lines (anti-juice-jacking / data-blocker mode) and clamps output voltage/current at five selectable thresholds to protect the downstream device from a malicious or faulty host/charger.
why_notable: Defensive USB-port protection device (data blocker + overvoltage/overcurrent cutoff combined); same general niche as already-tracked O.MG UnBlocker but a distinct, older product from a different maker.

name: unsurv offline
one_line: Small ESP32 board with GNSS receiver, accelerometer, and NFC tag interface; cross-references logged GPS tracks against an offline OpenStreetMap database of camera locations to generate a daily report of nearby surveillance cameras, with data read out over NFC.
why_notable: Purpose-built counter-surveillance/location-privacy logger (camera-proximity detection) combining GNSS and NFC in a way nothing in the tracked list does.

name: BusKill
one_line: Magnetic breakaway USB cable that functions as a laptop 'dead-man's switch': when physically yanked away from the user it triggers a user-configured action (screen lock, shutdown, or on Linux an optional LUKS-header wipe).
why_notable: Anti-seizure/anti-forensics physical-security gadget for snatch-and-run and border-search scenarios; conceptually adjacent to but functionally different from the tracked USBKill V4 (which electrically destroys the port rather than triggering a software response).

name: Ovrdrive USB
one_line: Open-hardware 8GB USB flash drive (ATtiny24A + SM3257ENT controller) that reads as blank storage unless plugged in three times in quick succession to unlock data access; includes a disabled-by-default circuit that can invert supply voltage to overheat the flash chip as a physical self-destruct trigger point.
why_notable: Anti-forensics/hidden-data storage device built for journalists/researchers in hostile environments, with an explicit hardware self-destruct hook; distinct niche from tracked forensic tools.

name: ESP32JTAG
one_line: Wi-Fi-connected JTAG/SWD debug probe combining an ESP32 and onboard FPGA, with a 16-channel 250MHz logic analyzer, FPGA bitstream programming, and a UART terminal, accessed through a built-in web server (no drivers needed).
why_notable: Wireless multi-function JTAG/SWD debug + logic-analyzer tool, a distinct device from any tracked debug probe (Tigard, Glasgow, Bus Pirate are all wired/USB).

name: HydraLink
one_line: USB 3.0 to Automotive Ethernet (100BASE-T1 / 1000BASE-T1) adapter that appears as a native Ethernet interface, letting standard tools (Wireshark, Scapy, tcpdump, bridge-utils) sniff, bridge, and manipulate in-vehicle Ethernet traffic such as SOME/IP and DoIP at wire speed.
why_notable: One of the first portable USB-to-automotive-Ethernet interfaces aimed explicitly at car hackers and pentesters fuzzing modern vehicle Ethernet networks, a layer the tracked automotive tools (which are CAN-focused) don't cover.

name: WiCAN
one_line: ESP32-C3 CAN-bus adapter (OBD-II or bare USB-CAN form factor) with Wi-Fi and BLE, exposing CAN traffic to RealDash, SavvyCAN, python-can/SocketCAN, and other libraries; power-saving sleep mode below 1 mA.
why_notable: Vendor's own description frames it explicitly 'for car hacking and general CAN-bus development'; a wireless, open-source CAN interface not currently in the tracked automotive set.

name: WiCAN Pro
one_line: ESP32-S3-based OBD-II scanner with a dedicated OBD interpreter chip supporting all legislated OBD-II protocols plus 3 CAN + 1 single-wire-CAN variants, USB-C flashing, microSD logging, and optional LTE/GPS add-on.
why_notable: Higher-tier sibling of WiCAN (same vendor) with broader protocol coverage; page explicitly names 'car hacking' as one hobbyist use case alongside diagnostics/Home Assistant, so the security framing is secondary to the base WiCAN.

name: GGtag
one_line: RP2040-based e-paper badge that emulates 125kHz RFID tags (ASK and FSK modulation) and is programmed over USB serial, a web-serial browser interface, or audio (ggwave), with a 3.52" e-paper display for the badge face.
why_notable: A novel form factor for RFID tag emulation (programmable e-paper badge, not a Proxmark/Chameleon/Flipper-style reader) not represented in the tracked RFID set.

name: QuadRF
one_line: 4x4 coherent MIMO SDR tile with an integrated Raspberry Pi 5 that measures signal arrival-time differences across four antennas to render a real-time augmented-reality overlay of RF sources (frequency-coded) on a phone/laptop camera feed at 30fps; can isolate and pass a selected signal to GNU Radio or other SDR tools.
why_notable: Vendor explicitly lists 'pinpoint hidden wireless cameras or rogue access points through walls' as a use case, making it an RF direction-finding/rogue-device-detection tool in the same spirit as the tracked KrakenSDR.

name: moRFeus
one_line: Field-configurable 30MHz-6GHz frequency mixer/converter and signal generator with an LCD/button interface and USB-HID programmability, toggling between mixer and standalone generator modes.
why_notable: Long-standing RF-hacking-community accessory used for shifting HackRF/SDR tuning ranges and RF experimentation; vendor's own use-case list explicitly names 'wideband jammers,' but the device itself is general-purpose lab RF gear.

name: RFGEN44
one_line: USB-powered, driver-free RF signal generator (ADF4351 synthesizer, PIC16 MCU) producing 35MHz-4.4GHz output in 10kHz steps, controllable via USB HID from Python/Matlab; currently a live crowdfunding campaign (14 days left at time of viewing, fully funded on a $1 goal).
why_notable: Generic hobbyist/lab RF signal source with no explicit security or offensive framing on its page; included only for the dual-use RF-testing potential common to this device class.

name: Sword of Secrets
one_line: Keychain-sized RISC-V board hosting a multi-stage hardware Capture-the-Flag challenge: solving it requires hardware reverse engineering, breaching protection registers over SPI/UART, and firmware-level exploitation; new stages are pushed as USB firmware updates.
why_notable: Dedicated hands-on hardware-hacking training device (successor to 'The Skull CTF') built around real embedded-exploitation techniques, a category not represented among tracked items.

name: GlitchCaster
one_line: Modular electromagnetic fault-injection (EMFI) probe head, based on the open PicoEMP design, that generates a roughly 250V EM pulse through a leaded or SMA probe coil; uses standard 40mm-fan mounting so it can be positioned by a 3D-printer/CNC XYZ stage for repeatable glitch targeting, with no built-in controller (bring your own GPIO/PWM controller).
why_notable: Distinct commercial EMFI tool built on the same open PicoEMP reference design as the tracked ChipSHOUTER-PicoEMP, but a different vendor/product aimed at CNC-mounted precision glitching; page has full specs but the project has not launched funding yet ('Coming Soon', no price/backers listed).

name: EPIC Erebus
one_line: M.2 2230 form-factor FPGA board (Lattice ECP5) built for PCIe DMA research/attacks; PCILeech-compatible, supports standalone memory acquisition and memory patch/match operations without a tethered host, fully open gateware/firmware/software toolchain.
why_notable: Purpose-built, compact PCILeech-class PCIe DMA-attack board from SecuringHardware.com (a hardware-hacking training company); occupies the same niche as the tracked Screamer PCIe Squirrel but is a distinct M.2 form-factor product. Project is 'Coming Soon' — not yet funded/launched, no price set.

name: ChipJabber Unplugged
one_line: DIY-buildable voltage fault-injection (glitching) kit with no programmable logic, offered in three build variants (through-hole kit, small SMD 'Mini' battery-powered unit, and a home-etch/PCB-mill-friendly board); pairs with an included 'NOTDuino' target board that demonstrates bypassing an EEPROM-keyed secure-boot check.
why_notable: Educational/DIY voltage-glitching kit from NewAE (maker of the tracked ChipWhisperer line) distinct from ChipWhisperer-Lite/Nano/Husky — a manual, knob-tuned glitcher rather than an automated FPGA-based one. Project is 'Coming Soon' — not yet funded/launched, no price set.

name: Negotchi - network security scanner
one_line: ESP8266 + OLED board that periodically scans the local WiFi network for hosts/vulnerabilities and runs a honeypot service; sounds an on-screen alarm if the honeypot is touched.
why_notable: Small standalone network-intrusion-detection gadget, a distinct category from the tracked wardriving/deauth boards.

name: Netgotchi Pro - Portable Network security scanner
one_line: Battery-powered ESP8266+OLED variant of Negotchi; scans WiFi for hosts/vulnerabilities, runs a honeypot, alarms on breach, configurable via onboard buttons or phone web portal.
why_notable: Portable/battery version of the same maker's network scanner line; distinct SKU worth tracking alongside Negotchi.

name: HackyPi - Programmable DIY USB Hacking Tool
one_line: RP2040-based USB stick with a 1.14in TFT and SD slot that emulates keyboard/HID input and runs drag-and-drop, cross-platform payload scripts (Python/HID libraries).
why_notable: Distinct BadUSB/HID-injection board with onboard display, not one of the already-tracked Digispark/CH552/pico-ducky designs.

name: USB Snake Box - Circuit Python Hacking Tool
one_line: CircuitPython microcontroller in a 3D-printed box with 4 buttons, each mapped to a different pre-programmed keystroke-injection (ducky-script-style) payload.
why_notable: Multi-button physical BadUSB variant, distinct form factor from tracked single-payload devices.

name: BLE BadUSB (JDY-08)
one_line: Atmega32U4 + JDY-08 BLE module USB stick that emulates a keyboard/mouse and accepts remote command injection over Bluetooth LE 4.0; open-source, Arduino-programmable.
why_notable: BLE-remote-triggered BadUSB, a different attack surface from the WiFi/onboard-payload devices already tracked.

name: BLE BadUSB (JDY-10)
one_line: Same design as the JDY-08 variant but with a JDY-10 BLE module; Atmega32U4 HID emulator remotely triggered over BLE.
why_notable: Same maker/product line as JDY-08 with a different BLE radio module — near-duplicate SKU, flagged for a human to decide whether to keep both.

name: Wifi BadUSB
one_line: Atmega32U4 + ESP-12F USB stick that acts as a HID injector and hosts its own WiFi access point for control/reflashing; runs supremeDuck/wifi_ducky/ESPloitV2 firmware.
why_notable: WiFi-controlled BadUSB from the same small maker, distinct hardware from the BLE variants above and from tracked devices.

name: Vidar attiny85 based BadUSB
one_line: Miniature ATtiny85 USB stick that emulates a keyboard and fires a pre-programmed keystroke payload (default: opens cmd + browser) on plug-in; firmware user-modifiable.
why_notable: Minimal, cheap ATtiny85 BadUSB from a different small maker than the tracked Digispark/CH552 boards.

name: Programmable BadUSB Payload Cable — USB-A to USB-C
one_line: USB-A-to-USB-C cable with an embedded microcontroller that emulates HID/mass-storage and stores multiple reprogrammable payloads; LED status indicator.
why_notable: Cable-form payload injector, conceptually similar to O.MG Cable but a different maker/product not already tracked.

name: Unlimited Coverage™ BAD USB Kit – USB Hacking Tool
one_line: Raspberry Pi Pico-based USB keyboard emulator kit with adapter cables and example scripts for keystroke-injection demos.
why_notable: Reseller kit built on RPi Pico HID emulation, functionally the same class of device as the tracked pico-ducky project.

name: ESP32 Network Toolbox
one_line: ESP32 board with Android companion app: scans WiFi, sniffs packets in promiscuous mode, sends deauth frames, runs an evil-twin captive portal, maps networks, scans BLE; exports PCAP/CSV/JSON.
why_notable: Full WiFi-pentest toolbox in one small board with an Android app; listing shows out-of-stock since Aug 2023 so supply should be double-checked.

name: Odiin: NFC Tag Emulation Toolkit
one_line: nRF52840-based handheld with 320x240 LCD that loads tag dump files from SD and emulates NFC-A tags (NTAG21X, partial MIFARE Classic/Ultralight) when tapped to a reader.
why_notable: Dedicated NFC tag-emulation handheld distinct from the tracked Chameleon/ACR122U/Proxmark devices.

name: PicoGlitcher v3
one_line: Raspberry Pi Pico 2-based voltage-glitching tool with two MOSFET crowbar outputs, 1.2-5V level shifters, and adjustable trigger filtering for fault-injection attacks on microcontrollers.
why_notable: Well-known open-source affordable alternative to ChipWhisperer for voltage glitching; not currently in the tracked list.

name: hs-probe
one_line: STM32F723-based open-hardware SWD/JTAG probe, CMSIS-DAP v1/v2 compatible, USB2.0 High-Speed with a USB mux for bootloader access; ships with ribbon cables and STDC10/14 connectors.
why_notable: Open-source high-speed debug probe from the well-known probe-rs project, distinct from the tracked Bus Pirate/Glasgow/Tigard probes.

name: XDS110 Debugger
one_line: Compact USB debug probe for TI MCUs/DSPs supporting JTAG, cJTAG, SWD and UART, with 5V/3.3V target power output; works with CCS/Keil/OpenOCD.
why_notable: Cheap dedicated JTAG/SWD probe for TI silicon, a niche not covered by the tracked general-purpose probes.

name: IBDAP - CMSIS-DAP JTAG/SWD Debug Adapter
one_line: NXP LPC11U35-based open-source USB debug adapter implementing CMSIS-DAP over JTAG/SWD, with UART/I2C/SPI peripherals for breakpoints, stepping and firmware download to ARM targets.
why_notable: Independent open-hardware JTAG/SWD adapter not currently in the tracked list.

name: Mini DAPLink Debug Probe
one_line: 3.2x1.7cm USB-C DAPLink probe for ARM Cortex-M targets (STM32/GD32/NRF51/52) over SWD/JTAG, plus a USB-serial UART bridge; enumerates as COM port + HID.
why_notable: Extremely low-cost dedicated SWD/JTAG probe, worth tracking as a budget option.

name: Open Source Portable USB Sniffer USB2.0
one_line: Board that captures USB 1.1/2.0 bus traffic at up to 48Mbps using open-source capture firmware, with 4 status LEDs; captures analyzed in Wireshark.
why_notable: Dedicated USB protocol-analysis hardware, a hardware-hacking niche not represented in the tracked list.

name: tinySniffer - USB sniffer
one_line: Inline pass-through device that captures full USB 1.x/2.0 enumeration and traffic between host and peripheral, remotely controllable, with disconnect/reconnect simulation and capture filtering.
why_notable: Remote-operable inline USB sniffer aimed at shipping the device to a target site for later analysis — a distinct use case from bench USB analyzers.

name: LittlePcap Network Tap/Packet Capture to USB drive
one_line: Inline dual-gigabit-Ethernet tap that writes captured traffic as PCAP files directly to an attached USB drive; USB-C powered, ~16s boot.
why_notable: Standalone-to-USB-drive network tap, distinct capture model from the tracked Throwing Star/Plunder Bug passive taps (which need a separate capture host).

name: Masterkey - WiFi USB Keylogger
one_line: Inline USB pass-through device (keyboard plugs into it, it plugs into the PC) that logs keystrokes internally, exposes a WiFi AP for wireless retrieval, and can also inject keystrokes/scripts.
why_notable: Combined hardware keylogger + HID-injection device from a known maker (JustCallMeKoko, also behind ESP32 Marauder), not currently tracked.

name: KEYVILBOARD - Wi-Fi
one_line: Inline hardware keylogger for QWERTY keyboards storing ~3M characters, retrievable over a 30m-range hidden WiFi network; supports remote key injection.
why_notable: Another distinct WiFi-exfil hardware keylogger, different maker/hardware from Masterkey and AirDrive.

name: EvilCrow-Keylogger
one_line: Inline USB keylogger built on Atmega32U4 + ESP32-PICO with a microSD slot; logs keystrokes to SD and exfiltrates over WiFi.
why_notable: Same maker/brand family as the tracked Evil Crow Cable/RF/Wind devices but a separate keylogger product not yet in the database.

name: NetNinja Wardriving GPS Marauder Flipper Zero
one_line: Flipper Zero expansion board combining an ESP32 with a battery-backed GPS module and 2.4GHz antenna; writes geotagged WiFi PCAPs to the Flipper's SD card, preloaded with Marauder firmware.
why_notable: GPS-tagged wardriving add-on for Flipper Zero, a capability not covered by the tracked Flipper Wi-Fi/multi boards.

name: Flipper Zero Wardriving GPS enabled ESP32 Board
one_line: ESP32 + external antenna + GPS receiver Flipper Zero add-on board, preloaded with Marauder firmware, in a 3D-printed case; connects via serial and logs to the Flipper's SD card.
why_notable: Same wardriving-GPS-for-Flipper concept as NetNinja above but a different maker/product — flagged so a human can pick one or track both.

name: ESP32 Marauder - Double Barrel 5G - C5 version
one_line: Dual-system board: a standalone ESP32 Marauder unit (touchscreen, battery, GPS) plus a second ESP32-C5 dual-band (2.4/5GHz) Flipper-controlled radio, with an added CC1101 sub-GHz chip and 4 external antennas.
why_notable: Adds genuine 5GHz WiFi scanning/deauth capability, which the currently tracked ESP32 Marauder v6.1/v7/v8 boards don't have.

name: DSTIKE Deauther32 Ultra
one_line: Dual-MCU handheld (ESP32-S3 + ESP32-C5) with two 1.54in color displays, dual antennas and a 3-cell 18650 battery; ESP32-S3 side does 2.4GHz scanning, ESP32-C5 side adds 2.4/5GHz WiFi6 scanning and deauth testing.
why_notable: Same maker/product family as the already-tracked "DSTIKE Deauther Watch" but a non-watch, dual-band flagship unit — flag for a human to decide if it's distinct enough to add separately.

name: Esp8266 WIFI Deauther
one_line: ESP8266 board that hosts an open "pwned" WiFi network and a web control interface at 192.168.4.1 for deauth-related testing.
why_notable: Small independent maker's basic ESP8266 deauther, distinct product from the tracked DSTIKE/ESP32 Marauder lines.

name: Wifi deauther PLUG PLAY Deauther ESP8266 v2.0
one_line: Pre-flashed NodeMCU board with a web-based (192.168.4.1) deauther UI supporting SSID spoofing, probe-request spam and deauthentication, powered via micro-USB.
why_notable: Another independently-branded pre-flashed NodeMCU deauther reseller, distinct listing from the tracked devices.

name: 2.4/5 GHz Deauther
one_line: RTL8720dn-based board hosting its own AP with a web UI; scans and deauths across both 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands, with an RGB status LED.
why_notable: Dual-band (2.4/5GHz) deauther using an RTL8720dn rather than ESP32/ESP8266 — different chipset from every tracked deauther. Listing shows "Product Retired" with no price, seller pointing to pcb-studios.com for current stock.

name: MSI.SDR 10kHz To 2GHz Panadapter SDR Receiver
one_line: 12-bit ADC SDR receiver covering 10kHz-2GHz with up to 10MHz bandwidth, 0.5ppm TCXO, SMA antenna port, micro-USB powered/data, aluminum enclosure.
why_notable: Wideband SDR receiver in a different product line from the tracked RTL-SDR/HackRF/KrakenSDR/PlutoSDR devices.

name: SDR-Rx Software Defined Radio Up Converter Module
one_line: HF upconverter/preamp board (10kHz-50MHz, with relay-switched VHF/UHF/SHF pass-through) that extends the low-frequency range of an existing RTL-SDR dongle; F and BNC connectors, USB powered.
why_notable: Adds real capability (HF reception) to existing SDR dongles but is an accessory rather than a standalone tool — included as a borderline call.

name: RTL-SDR Receiver w/ TCXO & Bias-T
